newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: SM Prime 1996 net boosted by economy.
newsitem.headline: SM Prime 1996 net boosted by economy.

text.p: SM Prime Holdings Inc, the Philippines' largest owner and developer of shopping malls, said on Tuesday gains in its 1996 results reflected increased consumer spending from a growing economy.
Earlier, SM Prime said its net profit rose by 27 percent to 1.914 billion pesos in 1996 from 1.510 billion pesos in 1995.
Gross revenues grew by 22 percent in 1996 to 3.769 billion pesos from 3.089 billion pesos in 1995, SM Prime said in a statement.
The 1996 earnings were in line with expectations of most analysts. In a Reuters poll in January, six securities firms forecast SM Prime's net at 1.914 billion pesos.
For this year, analysts expected SM Prime's profits to grow by 25.6 percent to 2.404 billion pesos.
"It was in line with forecast because of a 20 percent growth in rental income," Helen Alvarez, research director of All Asia Capital, said on Tuesday.
"It's a quality company. Its malls are well-positioned to benefit from increased spending on rising incomes," said Jose Salceda, director of SBC Warburg in Manila.
SM Prime has five shopping malls in the country, four of them in Metro Manila and one in Cebu, central Philippines. Its five malls have a gross floor area of 1.09 million square metres.
SM Prime said in its earnings statement that it is set to open two new malls every year for the next five years to take advantage of consumers' increased purchasing power.

An earlier report by All Asia Securities said SM Prime would represent the best play in the retail trade sector which is expected to grow by at least 15 percent per year as consumption expenditure expands.
Consumption spending accounts for 77 percent of the country's gross national product.
SM Prime added that it has a strong cash and financial position to fund its aggressive expansion and land acquisition programme over the next five years.
Analysts had said the company's cash-rich position, gained from a percentage of the sales of its tenants, had positioned it to ride on the increased consumer spending.
However, as a top-line company, it is one of the more expensive stocks on the Philippine Stock Exchange, analysts said.
At its closing price of 7.70 pesos on Tuesday, it is trading at 32 times forecast 1997 earnings versus the market's 17 times, SBC Warburg's Salceda said.
But Salceda added: "It's definitely not a sell. When you have a stock like this, you just allow earnings to grow."
"Strong earnings and strong operating cash flow justify the premium," agreed All Asia's Alvarez.
